source_caption:
One of the most powerful moments in The Crown is when Princess Diana visits a hospital and hugs a young boy living with AIDS.

To understand why this moment mattered so much, you have to remember what HIV/AIDS was like in the 1980s. Awareness was still very low, misinformation was everywhere, and fear of the disease was enormous. Many people wrongly believed HIV could be spread through ordinary physical contact, which led to people living with AIDS being isolated and treated with fear.

In 1987, Diana opened Britain’s first dedicated HIV/AIDS ward at Middlesex Hospital. During the visit, she shook hands with a patient without wearing gloves, directly challenging the idea that simply touching someone with HIV was dangerous. The image quickly became one of the most recognizable moments of her humanitarian work.

And Diana didn’t stop there.

In 1989, during a visit to Harlem Hospital in New York, she met children living with AIDS and picked up a seven-year-old boy, holding him in her arms. Once again, the cameras captured a moment that showed millions of people something they desperately needed to see: there was nothing frightening about human contact with someone living with HIV.

Diana’s actions didn’t cure AIDS or change public opinion overnight, and she wasn’t the only person fighting the stigma. Activists, doctors and public-health organizations had been working for years to educate the public. But her enormous visibility helped bring HIV/AIDS and the people affected by it into conversations around the world. She became one of the most recognizable public figures speaking openly against the stigma surrounding the disease.

That’s what makes these moments so powerful.

Diana used the cameras that followed her everywhere to focus attention on people the world was often afraid to even touch.
